title: Numbers and emergency calling
summary: E.164, emergency classifications, BYOC warnings, and Genesys Cloud Voice coverage.

lessons.title: Name the emergency owner before the DID
lessons.summary: Genesys is not responsible for emergency calls that ride a BYOC trunk. That sentence belongs in the design, not in the postmortem.
paras: The BYOC emergency article covers BYOC Cloud and BYOC Premises. You can dial the local emergency number, such as 911 in the United States, only after the carrier and the Genesys number plan and outbound route are both configured. If you also have Genesys Cloud Voice, its emergency information is not sent to the BYOC carrier. You tell the carrier the physical location yourself.

Under BYOC Cloud and some premises configurations the emergency path is on the internet. A power cut or a broadband cut can take it away. The article says that plainly. A design that assumes the Edge or the laptop will always reach a PSAP is not the article.

lessons.title: Emergency is a classification and a route
lessons.summary: The default Emergency plan matches 911 and 933 in the US and Canada, and 142 in Switzerland. It still needs a route.
paras: The number-plan article lists those defaults and the Suicide Prevention classification for 988 to +18002738255. Matching is not routing. The outbound route for the Emergency classification has to point at a trunk that can actually complete the call. An empty route is a matched number that goes nowhere.

933 is included alongside 911 in that default. Treat 933 as part of the documented US and Canada emergency classification, and re-read the page before you tell a tester which number to dial. Custom plans can shadow these defaults if you put a broader regex in front of them.

lessons.title: The location is a physical place
lessons.summary: The quick start adds a location because services, including emergency, need a real site.
paras: A location is not a division and not a site’s nickname. The BYOC quick start says you specify a physical location for the site, and the emergency article says the carrier needs the exact place the numbers are used. A downtown billing address for a warehouse an hour away is the kind of mistake that sends responders to the wrong door.

Global Media Fabric and the site’s Edges should agree with that same geography. A location in one city and a media path pinned across an ocean is a latency choice you should make on purpose, not by default.

lessons.title: Voice coverage is a table, not a promise
lessons.summary: Country rows decide DID, toll-free, domestic, and international. FedRAMP and the sovereign region add harder edges.
paras: The restrictions article is a matrix of countries and call types, plus two special sections. FedRAMP can add US numbers and US domestic and international calling, and it cannot add other countries. The European Sovereign region’s sovereignty commitment does not cover voice that leaves the ESR boundary. Those calls use non-EU carriers and are outside the commitment.

Planned regions on the Voice regions article, including notes about Mexico and Singapore in the table’s forward-looking rows, are not a contract. If the page says limited or coming, your design says limited or coming. The lab will not freeze that table.

lessons.title: Normalize toward E.164 on purpose
lessons.summary: Intra-country and inter-country plans normalize. Digit-length extensions and E.164 lists do not.
paras: The number-plan article is specific. Inter-country matches a country code and a length and normalizes to E.164. Intra-country uses the site’s country and does the same. Digit length for extensions does not normalize. An E.164 list entry must already contain the plus and is left alone. A number can pass through more than one plan and be normalized more than once.

That is why a double-prefix bug shows up as +1+1555… in a trace. A later plan normalized something an earlier plan had already finished. The call simulator is how you see it before the carrier rejects it.

lessons.title: Test emergency like a change, not like a demo
lessons.summary: A live emergency test is a carrier and public-safety conversation. The call simulator is the part you can do alone.
paras: Use the product call simulator for classification and normalization. Use a maintenance window and the carrier’s approved method before any live emergency test. The article’s warning about internet loss belongs in the test plan: if the broadband path is the only path, say what staff should do when it is down. That fallback is a life-safety procedure, and this lab will not invent a PSAP phone number for you.
Record the model, the location, the route, and the result. An unlogged successful test is a rumor. An unlogged failed test is how the next site repeats it.
